passages.t: The empty tomb, and words that seemed like nonsense
passages.happening:
Very early on the first day of the week, the women come to the tomb with the spices they had prepared. They find the stone rolled away, and when they go in, they do not find the body of the Lord Jesus (verses 1-3).

While they are puzzling over it, two men in shining clothes stand beside them. The women bow to the ground in terror. “Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee” (verses 5-6): the Son of Man must be handed over to sinful men, be crucified, and rise on the third day. “Then they remembered His words” (verse 8).

They go back and tell the Eleven and all the others. It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women. “But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women” (verse 11).

Peter, however, gets up and runs to the tomb. He bends down and sees only the linen cloths, and goes away, wondering what has happened (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
All four Gospels tell of the empty tomb, and the notes on Mark 16:1-8, Matthew 28:1-10 and John 20:1-18 explain it. In that world, a woman's word counted for less than a man's. Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, says that under Jewish law the testimony of women was not to be accepted (Antiquities 4.219). In the second century a critic of Christianity named Celsus mocked the resurrection as resting on the word of ‘a half-frantic woman’, as Origen reports in his reply. Yet all four Gospels agree that women were the first to find the tomb empty. Many historians think a story made up to convince people would hardly have chosen these witnesses.

Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James. Mary Magdalene and Joanna were among the women who had travelled with Jesus and supported him from their own means (8:2-3). They watched him die, saw where he was laid, and kept the Sabbath (23:49, 55-56). Now they are the first to hear.

Luke does not hide what happened next. The men thought it was ‘nonsense’. The Greek word, lēros, means idle talk, silly chatter. The first preachers of the resurrection were not believed, and the ones who did not believe were the apostles.

The angels do not begin with something to look at. They say ‘Remember’. Jesus had told them, more than once (9:22; 18:31-33). Luke's Gospel is full of words spoken and later understood.
passages.ot:
‘On the third day’ became part of the church's earliest confession. Paul, writing in the 50s, passes on that Christ “was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4). Some readers hear behind it Hosea's word: “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hosea 6:2).

The Law would not settle a matter on one person's word: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Luke gives several women, then Peter.
passages.hard:
Was verse 12 written by Luke? A few witnesses, Codex Bezae and some old Latin translations, leave it out. It is in the very old papyrus P75, copied around AD 200, in Codex Vaticanus, and in almost all other manuscripts. In 1881 Westcott and Hort judged it a later addition, but most scholars since have held that Luke wrote it, and modern Bibles print it. Later in the chapter the travellers to Emmaus say that “some of our companions went to the tomb” (verse 24), which fits it.

Do the Gospels disagree about the morning? They tell it in different ways: one angel or two, sitting or standing, which women came. The note on Matthew 28:1-10 sets out how readers explain this. What every account agrees on is the centre. Jesus died and was buried. On the first day of the week women found the tomb empty. They were told he had risen. And he appeared to his followers.
passages.asks: The women's words were called nonsense, and they had told the truth. Ask whose testimony you are quick to dismiss because of who they are. And notice Peter: he did not believe yet, but he ran to look. If you are not sure, you can still go and look.

passages.t: The road to Emmaus: “we were hoping”
passages.happening:
That same day two of the disciples are walking to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about everything that has happened. Jesus himself comes up and walks with them, “But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him” (verse 16).

He asks what they are discussing. They stand still, their faces sad. One of them, Cleopas, says, “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?” (verse 18). ‘What things?’ he asks. They tell him about Jesus of Nazareth, “a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people” (verse 19), and how the chief priests and rulers had him condemned and crucified. “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel” (verse 21). And now some women have told them of angels who said he was alive, and some of their friends found the tomb empty, “But Him they did not see” (verse 24).

Then Jesus says, “O foolish ones, how slow are your hearts to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (verses 25-26). “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story, and he tells it slowly. Two people are walking away from Jerusalem, the place where everything happened, at the end of the worst week of their lives. One is named Cleopas; the other is not named. Some have thought the second was his wife, but Luke does not say. Some also think Cleopas is the Clopas whose wife stood by the cross (John 19:25); a writer of the second century, Hegesippus, as quoted by Eusebius, said a Clopas was the brother of Joseph. That link is possible, but no one can be sure.

Where Emmaus was is not known. Several places have been proposed, and some manuscripts give a longer distance than seven miles (see the book page's map).

Listen to the three words in verse 21: ‘we were hoping’. They had hoped Jesus would set Israel free. Then they watched him die. The women's report has only confused them. They know all the facts, they even know the tomb is empty, and they are still walking away sad.

Jesus does not show them his hands first. He opens the Scriptures. ‘Was it not necessary’ uses Luke's word ‘must’, his word for God's plan. The cross was not the end of the hope. It was the way the hope came true.
passages.ot:
What did Jesus show them? Luke does not list the passages, and readers have guessed ever since. Christians have often pointed to passages such as the promise in Genesis that the woman's seed would “crush your head” (Genesis 3:15); the promise of “a prophet like me” (Deuteronomy 18:15); the servant who “was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5); and the psalm, “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10), which Peter quotes in Acts.

‘Moses and all the Prophets’ means the whole of the Jewish Scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament, not one or two verses.
passages.hard:
What does ‘beginning with Moses and all the Prophets’ claim? It claims that the whole story of Israel's Scriptures leads to a Messiah who suffers and then enters glory. It does not say that every verse is a hidden prediction, or that the Old Testament had no meaning for the people who first heard it. Christians explain the link in more than one way. Some stress prophecies that were fulfilled. Some stress patterns, people and events in Israel's story that point ahead, such as the Passover lamb. Some stress the shape of the whole story, of God's people suffering and being raised up. Many hold all three. These notes do not choose.

Jewish readers read the same Scriptures and do not find in them a crucified Messiah. They read them faithfully, in a long tradition of careful study. Christians may say plainly that they read these books differently, in the light of Jesus. They must never speak of Jewish readers with contempt. These were Israel's Scriptures first, and the two on the road were Jews, learning from a Jew to read their own Bible again.
passages.asks: If you are walking away disappointed, with ‘we had hoped’ in your mouth, this story is for you. You may have hoped God would fix something, and he did not, and you are tired. Jesus came alongside two people walking away. He let them say all of it. He did not scold them for their sadness; he scolded their slowness to trust what God had said. Ask whether you can tell him, honestly, what you had hoped. Then ask whether the thing that broke your hope might be part of a story you cannot yet see.

passages.t: Known in the breaking of the bread
passages.happening:
As they come near the village, Jesus acts as if he is going further. But they plead with him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over” (verse 29). So he goes in to stay with them.

At the table, “He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them” (verse 30). “Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus”, and he disappears from their sight (verse 31). They say to each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (verse 32).

That very hour they get up and go back to Jerusalem. They find the Eleven and the others, who say, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” (verse 34). Then the two tell what happened on the road, and how they recognised Jesus “in the breaking of the bread” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
In that world a traveller on the road at nightfall needed a place to stay, and offering one was a duty and an honour. Jesus does not force himself on them. He waits to be asked in. Luke's word for their ‘pleading’ is a strong one, like the ‘compel’ of the banquet parable (14:23), and here, as there, it means pressing an invitation, not force.

The guest becomes the host. He takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it, the same four actions as at the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and at the Last Supper (22:19). And at that moment they know him.

Notice the order of the story. First the hearts burn as the Scriptures are opened. Then the eyes are opened at the table. Luke puts the Word and the meal side by side.

Then they walk seven miles back, in the dark, the same day. Sadness made them slow. Joy makes them run. And when they arrive, before they can speak, they hear that Jesus has appeared to Simon. The prayer of 22:32 has been answered: Peter has been found.
passages.ot:
Abraham welcomed three strangers and set food before them, and found that he had welcomed the LORD (Genesis 18:1-8). The letter to the Hebrews later says that some have welcomed angels without knowing it.

The Psalms speak of God's word as light to the one who walks: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).
passages.hard:
Is ‘the breaking of the bread’ the Lord's Supper? Readers take it in more than one way. Some read the meal at Emmaus as the Lord's Supper itself, or as a picture of it: the risen Lord is known to his people when the bread is broken, and in Acts the first Christians devote themselves “to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42). Others read it as an ordinary evening meal in which Jesus did what he always did at table, and they knew him by it. Many hold both: an ordinary meal, told in words that Luke's readers would have heard at their own table of the Lord. Christians also differ, as on 22:19, about how Christ is present in that meal. These notes do not choose.

Why could they not recognise him? Luke says their eyes ‘were kept’ from it, and then ‘were opened’. He does not explain how. The point is that knowing Jesus is a gift. They could not see him until he gave them sight.
passages.asks: Their hearts were burning long before they understood why. Ask whether there has been a time when Scripture warmed you before it made sense to you. And notice what they did: they asked him to stay. Ask whether you have invited Jesus in, to your table, your evening, your ordinary life. He waits to be asked.

passages.t: “Touch Me and see”: flesh and bones, and a piece of fish
passages.happening:
While they are still talking, Jesus himself stands among them and says, “Peace be with you” (verse 36). They are startled and frightened, thinking they are seeing a spirit.

“Why are you troubled,” he asks, “and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see” (verses 38-39). A spirit, he says, “does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have”. He shows them his hands and feet.

They still cannot believe it, “because of their joy and amazement” (verse 41). So he asks, “Do you have anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he takes it and eats it in front of them (verses 41-43).
passages.hearers:
John tells of the same evening, with Thomas a week later (see the notes on John 20:19-29). Luke stresses one thing above all: the risen Jesus is not a ghost. Many people in that world believed that the spirits of the dead could appear. The disciples assume that is what they are seeing.

Jesus answers by offering his body. Hands and feet, where the nails went. Flesh and bones. And then something no ghost does: he eats. A meal with friends is the most ordinary proof there is.

Yet he is not simply the same as before. He appears in a closed room. He vanished from the table at Emmaus. His friends do not always know him at first. Christians have spoken of his risen body as truly a body, the same one that died, and also changed, no longer able to die. Paul calls it a body raised ‘in glory’ and ‘in power’ (1 Corinthians 15:43).

Luke's line ‘disbelieving for joy’ is honest. Sometimes good news is too good to take in at once.
passages.ot: The prophets hoped for a resurrection of the body, not only of the soul: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2). Isaiah promised, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).
passages.hard:
Was the resurrection a physical event, or a vision, or a way of saying his spirit lives on? Some have argued that the first disciples saw visions, or that ‘he is risen’ was a way of speaking about their faith. Luke writes against exactly that. His Jesus says, ‘It is I Myself’, invites touch, and eats. The Christian creeds confess the resurrection as an event that happened to Jesus' body, not as a picture of something that happened only in the disciples' minds. Christians who share that confession still wonder at how a risen body can be both the same and changed, and Scripture does not answer every question about it.

If you doubt, you are in good company. Luke says doubts arose in the disciples' hearts with Jesus standing in front of them. He did not send them away. He showed them his hands.
passages.asks: Jesus met frightened, doubting friends with ‘Peace be with you’, and then with a meal. Ask what doubts you are carrying, and whether you can bring them to him as they did. And ask what it means for your own body, your own death, and the bodies of those you have lost, that Jesus rose with flesh and bones.

passages.t: Repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem
passages.happening:
Jesus says to them, “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (verse 44). “Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (verse 45).

He tells them, “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things” (verses 46-48).

He is sending them the promise of his Father. “But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high” (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
‘The Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms’ are the three parts of the Jewish Bible (see the book page, ‘Luke and the Old Testament’). Jesus is saying the same thing he said on the road, now to all of them: the whole of Scripture points to him.

The message has three parts: the Messiah suffers, he rises, and in his name repentance and forgiveness are announced to every nation. Repentance means a change of mind and of life, the word John the Baptist preached at the start of the book (3:3). Forgiveness is the welcome Jesus gave to Zacchaeus, the lost son, and the criminal on the cross.

‘To all nations, beginning in Jerusalem’ is the plan of Luke's second book. In Acts Jesus says, “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The offer goes first to the city that crucified him. In Acts the first sermons are preached there, to the people of Jerusalem, and thousands believe.

‘The promise of My Father’ is the Holy Spirit, who comes at Pentecost in Acts 2.
passages.ot:
The prophets saw the nations coming to Israel's God. God says to his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). Isaiah saw many peoples saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD”, for the word would go out from Jerusalem (Isaiah 2:3). And Joel promised, “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).

Luke began his account of Jesus' work with Isaiah's words, “all humanity will see God’s salvation” (3:6). Now it begins to happen.
passages.hard:
Does ‘beginning in Jerusalem’ mean the message was for Gentiles instead of Jews? No. It begins with Jews, in Jerusalem, preached by Jews. Jesus does not turn away from his own city; he sends the offer of forgiveness there first. The nations are added, not swapped in. Paul would later write that the gospel is the power of God for salvation “to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

What does it mean that he ‘opened their minds’? Understanding Scripture, in Luke, is not only hard work. It is also a gift. The same Lord who opened the Scriptures on the road opens minds in the room.
passages.asks: Jesus sent his friends to start where they were, in the city where they had failed him. Ask where your ‘Jerusalem’ is: the place nearest to you, perhaps the hardest. And notice that they were told to wait for power before they went. Ask whether you are trying to do God's work on your own strength.

passages.t: He blessed them, and they returned with great joy to the temple
passages.happening:
Jesus leads them out as far as Bethany, lifts up his hands and blesses them. “While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven” (verse 51).

“And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, praising God continually in the temple” (verses 52-53).
passages.hearers:
Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, a little under two miles from Jerusalem. Jesus had come into the city from there (19:29). Now he leaves the world from there.

The last thing the disciples see is Jesus blessing them, with lifted hands, the way the priests of Israel blessed the people. Luke's book began with a priest, Zechariah, who came out of the temple and could not speak to the waiting people (1:21-22). Many readers think Luke means the reader to notice: the book that opened with a blessing that could not be spoken ends with a blessing given.

And it ends where it began, in the temple, with joy. The angel had promised ‘good news of great joy’ (2:10). Now the disciples, who were sad on the road and afraid in the room, are full of it. They worship Jesus, something faithful Jews gave to God alone, and they praise God in his house.

Luke tells the going up again at the start of Acts, at greater length. There he says Jesus appeared to them “over a span of forty days” (Acts 1:3) before he was taken up, and a cloud hid him.
passages.ot:
When Aaron the first high priest had offered the sacrifices, “Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them” (Leviticus 9:22). The priests' blessing was given in God's own words: “May the LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24).

The Psalms see God's king going up in triumph: “God has ascended amid shouts of joy” (Psalm 47:5).
passages.hard:
Did Luke write ‘and was carried up into heaven’? The words are missing from Codex Bezae, some old Latin translations and Codex Sinaiticus. Most manuscripts have them, and most modern Bibles print them. Some think they were dropped because Luke here seems to place the going up on Easter evening, while Acts speaks of forty days. Either way, Luke's own second book tells plainly of the ascension (Acts 1:9).

Does Luke contradict Acts about when Jesus went up? Readers answer in more than one way. Many think Luke's Gospel tells the end of the story briefly, without saying how many days passed between verses 49 and 50, and that Acts fills it in. Others think Luke shaped the two endings for two purposes: the Gospel closes the story of Jesus, Acts opens the story of the church. The same writer wrote both, and did not think they clashed.

What does the ascension mean? Not that Jesus went away into the sky and is far off. It means he went to the Father, to the place of all authority, as the creeds say: he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. And he will come back in the same way (Acts 1:11).
passages.asks: The disciples went back to the city where Jesus had been killed, and they went with joy. Nothing outside had changed. They had. Ask what it would look like to carry that joy into the place where your own hard things happened. And remember the last picture Luke gives of Jesus: his hands lifted, blessing. That is how he left them, and that is how he holds his people still.
